entries.title: Why is Germany building roads for yesterday's climate?
entries.summary: As heat waves buckle its Autobahn, Germany is still paving roads for a past climate. Engineers know how to fix it — so what's the holdup?
entries.content:
July 28, 2026

As heat waves buckle its Autobahn, Germany is still paving roads for a past climate. Engineers know how to fix it — so what's the holdup?

Multi-day European heat waves with temperatures topping 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius) are increasingly leaving their mark on Germany's famed Autobahn — buckling concrete slabs, deforming asphalt, and forcing temporary speed limits.

In early July alone, seven stretches of the country's highways had to be shut down completely for a time.

"The cause often lies in the bitumen — the petroleum-derived binder in asphalt. It's elastic and can soften at high temperatures, from around 60 degrees Celsius," a spokesperson from Autobahn GmbH, the company that manages Germany's highways, told DW. Bitumen is a component in most of the country's roads.

When outdoor temperatures climb above 30C, the surface of dark asphalt can quickly heat to double that or more in the sun and then deform. Using modern, bitumen-free asphalt mixes lowers the risk of such damage, according to Autobahn GmbH.

So, as heat waves intensify and traffic volumes rise, are Germany's roads built to last?

Autobahn need to be prepared for the heat

German roads are "not designed for these stresses at all," said Nina Stelzenmüller. The engineer heads the road construction technology division at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in southwestern Germany. "The composition of the road surface is based on experience from the last 30 or 50 years," and not on the increasingly noticeable shifts in the climate, explained Stelzenmüller.

At present, road surfaces have to be designed for a temperature range of minus 30C to plus 45C, according to Autobahn GmbH. They are built, the company said, to withstand "the climatic stresses from heat and cold to be expected in Germany."

Yet in some regions of eastern Germany, temperatures could exceed that 45C maximum on certain days by at least 2040. That's according to climate models from Germany's National Meteorological Service (DWD), which assume emissions will remain high in the coming years and that global warming will continue to intensify.

A studyinvolving the research institute of Germany's federal transport ministry (BASt) likewise concludes that climate change is already pushing existing road materials to their limits, and that action is needed. But these findings have not yet translated into binding requirements for updating street surfaces.

Resurfacing as an opportunity: Climate-ready asphalt for the future

Every road resurfaced today needs to withstand temperatures that may only become reality decades from now. But there are plenty of ways to make Germany's vital road infrastructure heat-resistant for the medium to long-term.

A 2019 study, also involving BASt, found that dark asphalt heated up by 7C less when light-colored quartzite was mixed in. The researchers recommended applying reflective surface layers to roads and building in other cooling materials as quickly as possible. The study did not examine the cost or durability of such heat adaptations.

According to Autobahn GmbH, lighter-colored stone is already being used in construction in some cases. The regional availability and cost of such stone also play a role in its use, said the company.

Individual states and cities are also testing and planning light-colored road surfaces, including in the western German cities of Oberhausen and Stuttgart, as well as the eastern state of Brandenburg.

Just scattering light-colored quartzite over the asphalt surface could also help, according to Stelzenmüller, and would be a short-term, feasible approach.

Global models: Water in the asphalt and reflective coatings

Germany isn't alone in facing increasingly hot roads. Infrastructure needs to be adapted worldwide.

Tokyo, for example, already uses reflective, water-retaining road surfaces as standard when resurfacing streets. These can lower the surface temperature by 8 to 10 degrees Celsius. By 2030, some 152 miles (245 kilometers) of roads in the Japanese capital are to be fitted with them.

In Phoenix, in the United States, light-colored coatings have also already been applied to numerous streets. They reflect more sunlight, so absorb less heat. During the day, they were around 6.7C cooler than conventional surfaces. But at the same time, this noticeably warmed the ambient air for passersby.

But Germany, like many other countries, is still a long way from the systematic use of suitable road surfaces to combat heat damage. And even as average temperatures keep rising, the challenge remains that the road surface also has to stay stable even in freezing winter conditions.

As an alternative to bitumen, high-performance binders that can survive both extremes — frost and heat — are currently being developed, said Stelzenmüller.

"For one thing, they're especially elastic, so that at low temperatures they can still bear the stresses caused by the cold. But at the same time they also have a very high strength, which allows them to withstand deformation at high temperatures," explained the engineer.

Policy lags behind the research

A great deal of research on climate-adapted road construction already exists, according to Stelzenmüller.

"But by the time these findings are actually written into regulation and roads are routinely built with them — that's a process that will take years if not decades. I don't expect it can be implemented in the next two or three years," she added.

The heat-ready overhaul of the infrastructure could happen faster if the transport ministry and the road-construction authorities pushed the issue. That's what happened with the tightening of pollutant limits in the development of asphalt mixes.

In 2025, Germany's transport ministry ordered that less-toxic surfaces be adopted "as quickly as possible," even before a new directive on the issue officially took effect.

"There was a real sense of urgency to meet those limits. And here it worked out [quickly], establishing new regulations within a few years," she said.

For road construction that is adapted to climate change and fit for the future, authorities need to take a similar approach, said Stelzenmüller.

"If you put a stronger focus on it, you could certainly have new types of asphalt within a few years," Stelzenmüller added.

By the time of publication, Germany's transport ministry had not responded to DW's request for comment.

This article was translated from German by Josh Axelrod.

entries.title: Japan: Strong earthquake hits Kumamoto, many feared dead
entries.summary: Dozens of people were hospitalized after the earthquake hit southern Japan. According to media reports, many are feared dead after a shopping mall partially collapsed in the town of Kashima.
entries.content:
Japan

Japan: Strong earthquake hits Kumamoto, many feared dead

July 28, 2026

Dozens of people were hospitalized after the earthquake hit southern Japan. According to media reports, many are feared dead after a shopping mall partially collapsed in the town of Kashima.

A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture on Japan's southern island of Kyushu on Tuesday afternoon, triggering emergency warnings and prompting authorities to assess the extent of the damage.

Japan's public broadcaster, NHK, reported that "many people" were trapped inside an Aeon shopping mall damaged by the earthquake. Earlier, local police reported an explosion at the mall in Kashima Town.

According to local broadcaster TBS, police said "quite a few" were presumed dead in the incident.

Meanwhile, NHK reported that at least 50 people were hospitalized after the earthquake.

Authorities assess damage as tsunami threat eases

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also said initial reports indicated multiple injuries, damage to civilian infrastructure, and fires in several affected areas.

"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Takaichi said.

"Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed," she added.

Although the earthquake caused widespread disruption and temporarily raised fears of a tsunami, officials later confirmed that the threat had subsided and that Japan's coastline was no longer in danger.

"This earthquake occurred inland, and no tsunami activity has been observed so far," a spokesperson for the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said. "For this reason, we hope to lift the tsunami advisory at a relatively early stage, depending on future sea level conditions."

Power and nuclear facilities remain safe

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority reported that no abnormalities were detected at three nearby nuclear power plants, providing reassurance in a country still sensitive to nuclear safety concerns following the 2011 Fukushima disaster.

However, the earthquake disrupted electricity supplies across the region. According to Kyushu Electric Power, approximately 45,000 households and facilities in Kumamoto temporarily lost power following the tremor.

Several major industrial facilities are located near the earthquake zone, including operations belonging to Sony and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker. Sony stated that it was evaluating conditions at its facilities, while TSMC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Japan's long history of major earthquakes

Kumamoto is no stranger to devastating seismic events.

In 2016, the region was struck by two major earthquakes, first a magnitude 6.5 quake and then a magnitude 7.3 tremor two days later. The disaster claimed 273 lives, injured more than 2,800 people. Thousands of buildings were either damaged or destroyed, making it one of Japan's most destructive recent earthquake disasters.

More recently, a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck northern Japan on June 25, causing little damage and no fatalities. Earlier this year, on April 20, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in northern Japan injured at least ten people and shook high-rise buildings as far away as Tokyo, prompting authorities to issue a temporary advisory warning of an increased risk of even stronger earthquakes. That advisory was lifted a week later.

One of the world's most earthquake-prone nations

Japan sits along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire," one of the most active seismic zones on Earth where four major tectonic plates meet.

Home to approximately 125 million people, the country experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year and accounts for roughly 18% of the world's seismic activity.

While most tremors are relatively minor, Japan remains haunted by memories of the catastrophic magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami that struck the country's northeast coast in March 2011. The disaster killed or left missing around 18,500 people and triggered the Fukushima nuclear crisis.

Tuesday's earthquake demonstrated the country's preparedness systems, emergency response capabilities, and monitoring of critical infrastructure. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi office also posted a safety guideline on X, assuring that their safety remains their top priority.

As authorities continue to assess the impact of the Kumamoto quake, residents are being urged to stay alert for potential aftershocks and follow official safety guidance.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Will Pakistan intervene amid Houthi attacks on Saudi ships?
entries.summary: Pakistan and Saudi Arabia are strategic defense partners, but experts say there are limits to how far Islamabad can go in opposing Iran-backed Houthis.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Will Pakistan intervene amid Houthi attacks on Saudi ships?

July 28, 2026

Pakistan and Saudi Arabia are strategic defense partners, but experts say there are limits to how far Islamabad can go in opposing Iran-backed Houthis.

Pakistan condemned attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea by Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi militia last week as the conflict in the Middle East threatens to expand.

In a statement, the Pakistani Foreign Ministry warned that any Houthi threat to Pakistani maritime interests in the Red Sea could be met with the "lawful use of force."

Pakistan enjoys a trade and security relationship with Saudi Arabia, and Pakistani-flagged vessels frequent Saudi ports in the Red Sea. Last September, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a mutual defense agreement that contains a "collective security" clause, meaning attack on one country is considered an attack on both.

After the Houthis launched missiles at southern Saudi Arabia last week, Pakistan's Foreign Ministry expressed its "unwavering commitment" to the security pact.

At the same time, Pakistan also has ties with Iran, and has been a key mediator between Tehran and Washington to end the Iran war.

Any military act against the Iran-backed Houthis could place Islamabad in one of the most complicated foreign policy situations it has faced in years.

Pakistan's tightrope between Saudis and Iran

Historically, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have shared close military and strategic relations. Pakistani military generals and advisers have aided the kingdom for decades.

Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen expert at London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW that Pakistani troops are already in Yemen in support of the Saudis, "carrying out security and training-related duties alongside Saudi forces."

A Pakistani official DW spoke to categorically denied this claim.

Nevertheless, if Houthi attacks on oil tankers and commercial shipping escalate in the Red Sea, Saudi Arabia could turn to Pakistan for help.

"Pakistan is one of Riyadh's closest defense partners, and their mutual defense pact makes such a request plausible. Having also come under Iranian attack, Saudi Arabia may increasingly look to Islamabad for military assistance if it feels under growing security pressure," Michael Kugelman, senior fellow at the Washington-based Atlantic Council, told DW.

However, Pakistan's improving ties with Iran and its mediation to end the US-Iran conflict could complicate any Pakistani military role on Saudi Arabia's behalf. 

"Pakistan and Iran have a complicated relationship based on the calculation of tactical gains by either side. In any case, Pakistan has warned Iran several times that in case of conflict it will support Saudi Arabia," Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani military analyst and senior fellow at King's College London, told DW.

After a period of unprecedented tensions in 2024, when Iran and Pakistan exchanged cross-border missile strikes, the neighbors have since rebuilt diplomatic relations and strengthened cooperation against militant groups operating along their shared border.

"Limited military support for Saudi Arabia would not necessarily rupture Pakistan's ties with Iran. But at a time when Islamabad is trying to present itself as a neutral mediator, expanding arms support to Riyadh could deepen Tehran's suspicions and undermine Pakistan's diplomatic role," Kugelman said.

How much support can Pakistan give?

If Saudi Arabia seeks assistance, analysts say Pakistan's contribution would most likely focus on protecting Saudi interests rather than joining offensive operations.

"The preference would be for defensive engagement, as expanding operations in the Red Sea may prove too risky," said Siddiqa.

Such an approach could include intelligence sharing, air-defense cooperation, maritime surveillance and protecting critical Saudi infrastructure, allowing Pakistan to support Riyadh without joining offensive operations.

"Despite its deep military ties and mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan is unlikely to provide arms or troops. Islamabad is focused on preventing regional escalation and preserving its role as a mediator in the Iran conflict, making any military support for Riyadh politically risky and potentially damaging to its ties with Tehran," said Kugelman.

Will Saudi Arabia escalate?

Saudi Arabia has exercised considerable restraint since winding down its large-scale military campaign in Yemen. However, repeated attacks on oil infrastructure and commercial shipping may eventually force Riyadh to respond more aggressively.

"Continued Houthi attacks on Saudi vessels could prompt Riyadh to abandon its restraint and launch a military response," said Al-Muslimi.

King's College analyst Siddiqa said it is not clear that Saudi Arabia currently has the capacity to fight a prolonged sub-conventional war against the Houthis.

"While it may intensify air strikes, more bombardment alone is unlikely to achieve the objective of making the kingdom more secure," she said.

The analysts agreed Islamabad will likely back maritime security and freedom of navigation while avoiding direct strikes on Houthi targets amid the looming US-Iran conflict. But if the Red Sea conflict escalates, staying neutral may become increasingly difficult as pressure from Riyadh and Tehran grows.

"The trajectory of the conflict with Iran will shape Saudi Arabia's tolerance for Houthi attacks," said Kugelman.

"If the current pause between the US and Iran holds, Riyadh is likely to wait out the attacks rather than escalate. But Saudi Arabia will continue to view Pakistan as a key security partner because Houthi attacks are unlikely to stop, even if the Iran conflict ends," he added.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Germany: Online tourist accommodation bookings hit new peak
entries.summary: Vacation rental bookings through online platforms have climbed to a new record in Germany. The figures reveal major regional differences in where certain tourists like to go.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Online tourist accommodation bookings hit new peak

July 28, 2026

Vacation rental bookings through online platforms have climbed to a new record in Germany. The figures reveal major regional differences in where certain tourists like to go.

Bookings for tourist accommodation in Germany through major online platforms have reached a record high.

The figure rose sharply above both last year's level and figures seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Why are tourist rental bookings rising in Germany?

Travellers booked 68.3 million overnight stays through Airbnb, Booking.com and Expedia in 2025, the Federal Statistical Office said on Tuesday, citing data from EU statistics agency Eurostat.

That was an increase of 13% compared with 2024 and more than 83% above the level recorded in 2019.

The rise came despite TripAdvisor no longer being included in the data after it left the short-term accommodation booking market.

Strong domestic demand was the main driver of growth. German travellers booked 48.5 million overnight stays, an increase of more than 15% from the previous year.

The number of domestic bookings has more than doubled since 2019.

Foreign visitors booked 19.8 million overnight stays, almost 8% more than in 2024.

Who is visiting Germany's tourist spots?

Travellers from the Netherlands accounted for the largest number of international bookings, with 2.9 million overnight stays, followed by Poland with 2.1 million and the US with 1.3 million.

The figures largely reflect the market for smaller and privately operated accommodation.

Around 94% of booked nights were spent at properties with fewer than 10 beds, which are not included in Germany's official monthly tourism statistics.

The platform data therefore provide a broader picture of the country's short-term accommodation market.

Bavaria recorded the highest number of overnight stays, with 10.6 million. Baden-Württemberg and North Rhine-Westphalia followed with 8.1 million each.

Travel patterns varied considerably between Germany's states.

Around 90% of guests in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Schleswig-Holstein came from within Germany, while city-states and western regions attracted a larger share of international visitors.

Foreign guests accounted for more than two-thirds of bookings in Berlin, at 67.7%.

Their share was also above average in North Rhine-Westphalia, at 42.3%, and Baden-Württemberg, at 40.8%.

entries.title: 'Loneliness influencers': Being alone brings in the clicks
entries.summary: No friends, no dating, no problem? Many influencers are presenting social isolation as a lifestyle. But experts warn of the consequences.
entries.content:
July 28, 2026

No friends, no dating, no problem? Many influencers are presenting social isolation as a lifestyle. But experts warn of the consequences.

A young woman in business attire comes home, cuddles with her cat, cleans her high heels, takes a shower and settles down on the couch to watch TV in her pajamas with pizza and a soft drink. Afterward, she tidies up, takes out the trash ("no clutter in this apartment ever") and spends the rest of the evening on the sofa with her cat.

The title of the video: "POV: You live alone in NYC and have no friends so this is how you spend your Friday night." It has already raked in over 11 million views on Instagram.

This reel is the most successful clip to date by Paulina Cee, who boasts over 320,000 followers on Instagram.

Her account features numerous videos of this kind, always emphasizing her friend-free life.

And Paulina Cee is just one influencer amid a broader trend: Social media is full of young women presenting their solitude as a lifestyle. Sometimes they have a dog, sometimes one or two cats, but otherwise the videos share a similar aesthetic: an apartment so clean and so sparsely furnished, it verges on sterility.

At peace with themselves and being alone

One of the pioneers of this trend is Lana Isa from Toronto. Her videos bear such titles as "just an introvert in her natural habitat (home alone with yummy food)" or "what a weekend looks like as a friendless girl with NO interest in men or dating."

Lana Isa always ends her reels with the positive message, "Enjoy your life." She appears to be at peace with her largely solitary lifestyle. Apart from FaceTime calls with her mother and contact with her sister, her clips mainly revolve around consumption: usually unhealthy food, new clothes or movies.

The Canadian says her content has no purpose other than sharing her real life, which, according to her, has been shaped by generalized anxiety disorder and the loss of her relationship and all of her friendships several years ago.

It was never supposed to be just an 'aesthetic vlog,' or to romanticize having no friends. ... I just happened to start filming and show the current chapter of my life, which was the peace that came after I dealt with my feelings."

Authenticity hard to verify

Mareike Ernst, an assistant professor of psychoanalytically-oriented psychotherapy research at the University of Klagenfurt, has mixed feelings about such reels.

Ernst, whose research focuses on psychotherapy and loneliness, says that on the one hand, it is positive when young women show that being alone, even in public, is good and normal: "That can help destigmatize it and provides a counterpoint to the content of many other influencers, who often portray almost constant social interaction."

On the other hand, young people in similar life situations might view these "loneliness influencers" as role models, "so that it becomes increasingly normalized to spend most of your time alone and convince yourself that 'this is perfectly fine.'"

Whether these loneliness influencers are all truly authentic is difficult to verify. What matters, however, is that many followers believe them and respond positively to the solitary lifestyle shown in the videos. The fact remains: Prolonged social isolation can make people ill. Studies show that it increases the risk of heart disease, mental illness and premature death.

More and more young people are exposed to these risks. In a 2025 World Health Organization (WHO) study, between 17% and 21% of respondents aged 13 to 29 said they felt lonely, with the highest rates observed among teenagers. The WHO estimates that around one quarter of them are affected by social isolation. According to a Nivea study conducted in 13 countries, 24% of young people aged 16 to 24 feel socially isolated, compared with 19% across all age groups.

Solitude as an aesthetic?

"Loneliness influencers" are almost exclusively women. Ernst suspects this has to do with gender stereotypes: Women are expected to build relationships and be there for others. This countertrend may therefore constitute a form of emancipation.

"Or perhaps it simply fits better with the female influencer aesthetic, which often focuses on self-care, cooking, tidying up and similar activities."

Because of this aesthetic, US psychotherapist Phil Lane recently addressed these influencers in an Instagram post. "Loneliness influencers, stop trying to make loneliness as an aesthetic happen; it is not going to happen. It is important that we are around our fellow human beings. It's one of our basic human needs."

Lane stressed that there is nothing wrong with spending time alone. "Sometimes, I really enjoy my own company, and I enjoy solitude, but we can't overapply this because it can have significant health risks."

So far, however, his message has gained little traction: His post has garnered only around 900 views.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Bernadette Amani 'living her dream' at Bayern and WAFCON
entries.summary: Bernadette Amani joined Bayern Munich in January and is now captaining Ivory Coast in their first WAFCON in 12 years. Getting to the top hasn't been a straight path for the newly crowned German double winner.
entries.content:
Cote d'Ivoire

Bernadette Amani 'living her dream' at Bayern and WAFCON

July 28, 2026

Bernadette Amani joined Bayern Munich in January and is now captaining Ivory Coast in their first WAFCON in 12 years. Getting to the top hasn't been a straight path for the newly crowned German double winner.

Seven months after moving to Germany, Bernadette Amani is clearly where she wants to be, having won both the Bundesliga and the German Cup in her first half-season since joining Bayern Munich.

"It's a dream come true for me to be here, and I'm living my dream to the full," the 28-year-old midfielder told DW in an exclusive interview shortly before the Women's Africa Cup of Nations kicked off in Morocco this month.

"Munich is a very, very big club. Beyond just making me happy, it's a real achievement, a dream come true to be here, to play for such a prestigious club."

Amani added that playing for Bayern's women has been a major step up from what she had come to know playing for CD Tenerife Femenino of Liga F, Spain's topflight.

"I was already professional when I was in Spain, but let's just say it wasn't quite the same level of professionalism," she explained.

"In Spain or the Ivory Coast, the coaching staff might have consisted of no more than five or six people. But here there are eight or 10 people. And that enables them (the players) to perform at that high level for a long time."

This structure, and the experience of the players around her, she said, make it virtually impossible for a new player not to improve on their own game.

"I've learned a great deal about aspects I wasn't already aware of; how to position myself, how to position my body, how to interact with the ball and how to think. Really understanding the game is something I'm gradually learning alongside (the players) and the coaching staff."

Moving to the capital to further education

Getting to the Bundesliga champions was anything but a straight, plotted path for Amani, who, when she began kicking a ball with the boys in her local village as a youngster, had no idea that football could be a career option.

Her parents were anything but encouraging of her passion. They just wanted their daughter to get a good education. To this end, she wound up moving from the village of Dougbafla, where she grew up, to the capital, Abidjan — a move that turned out to be pivotal to her career as a footballer.

"I discovered the women's football league. I went to a match and, as luck would have it, it was the top team against the second-placed team," she recalled.

"I saw the intensity, I saw the technique, and then I heard that so-and-so isn't here today because she's playing in Serbia, another isn't here today because she's playing in Turkey. And that was a real eye-opener for me; it made me realize that I could make a living from what I love."

One of the clubs she watched on that day in 2019, Onze Soeurs de Gagnoa, offered her a trial – and she made it. Within a year, she was in Spain's third tier, and five years later, she found herself in Liga F with Eibar. Always looking to take that next step, she quickly moved on to Tenerife, her launching pad for Bayern, which she describes as "the top." Still, there's no question of complacency.

"Someone on the outside will say to you: 'You've put in the effort, you've made it to Bayern, a club that wins titles, that's professional and renowned all over the world," she said.

"But someone who's involved in football will tell you that's where the hard part begins. Staying there is even better. And it's hard not to let your guard down."

Top three the goal at WAFCON

For the next couple of weeks though, her focus will be on her role as captain of Ivory Coast at the Women's Africa Cup of Nations. WAFCON 2026, for which Ivory Coast were one of four late additions after the tournament was expanded from 12 to 16 teams at the last minute, marks the country's return to the continental competition after an absence of 12 years.

"The target that has been set for us is, of course, to do no worse than we did at the last Africa Cup of Nations we took part in — that is, to finish third," she said.

Amani noted that while Ivory Coast now have more players in top leagues in Europe than in 2014, almost half the squad will stand to make their first appearance at a WAFCON. Still, she appeared quietly optimistic.

"We're going to focus on our own game, and we know that we've got qualities that could give (our opponents) a run for their money," she said.

The Lady Elephants did more than that in Casablanca on Monday, cruising past Burkina Faso 4-1 in their opening match, putting them top of Group B. Their second match, on Friday against South Africa, ranked second on the continent, could provide Amani's side with a sterner test – despite South Africa having been upset 2-1 by lowly Tanzania in their opener.

Ali Farhat contributed to this article.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

entries.title: As US-Iran war rages, who's risking the Strait of Hormuz?
entries.summary: Though Iran continues to attack vessels as leverage in its war with the United States, data show that several shippers continue to transit the waterway.
entries.content:
Middle East

As US-Iran war rages, who's risking the Strait of Hormuz?

July 28, 2026

Though Iran continues to attack vessels as leverage in its war with the United States, data show that several shippers continue to transit the waterway.

The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the world's most dangerous waterways since March, when Iran began attacking shipping vessels as a pressure tactic in its ceasefire talks with the United States. Still, though a significant proportion of the global oil trade bottlenecks at the strait, shipping traffic never completely halted.

With the United States and Iran issuing conflicting statements as to whether the Strait of Hormuz is open, DW analyzed public data sources to track how shipping traffic has changed during the course of the war and which vessels are still taking the risk of transiting the maritime choke point, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. 

Shipping through Strait of Hormuz disrupted

As Iran's strikes on and interception of vessels in the Strait of Hormuz continue, mines have also been reported in the prewar shipping lanes. 

The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), a project of the US-led Combined Maritime Forces, assesses the threat to shippers as "severe," its second-highest warning level. However, according to one of JMIC's latest advisory notes, issued after attacks resumed on July 6 and 7, "commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained at reduced levels, with vessels transiting via both the southern Omani corridor and the northern Iranian-controlled route."   

JMIC added that shippers remained cautious of transiting the strait amid the attacks on vessels in recent weeks.

DW's analysis of data from the open-source platform Global Fishing Watch showed that, nevertheless, several shipping companies have navigated their vessels through the Strait of Hormuz throughout the war. Though the platform's primary purpose is to monitor fishing efforts, it also collects data on all other vessels using satellite imagery and relying on signals transmitted by ships' automatic identification systems (AIS).

As ships can switch off their AIS transponders — and have reportedly repeatedly chosen to while transiting the Strait of Hormuz — the number of vessels is likely higher than shown.

Based on AIS signals, a combined total of at least 84 ships crossed the Strait of Hormuz in two periods of the conflict: from the start of the war on February 28 until the announcement of a ceasefire on April 7 and following the renewed attacks on July 6 and 7. This aligns with reports of the United States saying it gave passage to about 70 ships and adding that not all of them transmitted signals.  

For comparison: In the same periods of 2025, more than 900 ships crossed the strait.

Of these 84 ships, 34 moved from east to west into the Persian Gulf and 50 crossed the strait in the opposite direction, moving out of the gulf.

In which countries are ships that transit the Strait of Hormuz registered?

As part of the AIS signal, ships transmit which flag they are sailing under, but this information is entered manually aboard the vessels. In only a few cases investigated for this story did the flag reflect the actual country of origin of the registered owner or the ship manager of a vessel. This information can still be looked up manually in different databases using the ship's international ID number and its name.

Only nine Iranian- and two Pakistani-owned ships transited under their respective national flags. All of the other 73 ships hoisted a flag different from the vessel owner's country. 

Analysis of this data shows that a wide variety of companies operating in the region continue to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

At the top of the list is the United Arab Emirates, which neighbors the strait. The UAE's Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP) runs overland parallel to the waterway in the south. 13 cargo ships registered in the United Arab Emirates transited the strait during the shutdown, as well as two liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tankers and three support vessels.  

Most of the UAE-based ship owners in the dataset appear to have only one to five vessels in their fleet. One of the UAE-registered vessels that was detected passing into the Persian Gulf on July 11 is managed by Lubeck Shipping LLC, a company associated with an Iranian oil tycoon that has been sanctioned by the United States.  

Also sanctioned by the United States is Salina Ship Management PvT Ltd., a company from the Indian state of Maharashtra that US officials accuse of helping Iran move petrol. The company manages one of the four Indian oil and LPG tankers that Global Fishing Watch recorded entering the strait.  

India, like many Asian countries, is heavily reliant on the Strait of Hormuz for energy supply. China, Pakistan and Vietnam, too, had oil and LPG tankers in the Persian Gulf that they moved out of the Strait of Hormuz before a ceasefire was announced on April 7. 

All seven vessels owned and managed by companies from Greece, the world's biggest shipping power, were freighters, typically carrying unpackaged dried goods such as iron, coal and grains. 

Why risk transiting the Strait of Hormuz?

The primary motive for continuing to move oil and other goods via the Strait of Hormuz despite the threat of attacks by Iran is financial — "simply because the reward seems higher than the risk," said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler, a business intelligence company headquartered in Belgium that specializes in analyzing global commodity flows.  

"The key point is that producers of oil (or gas, aluminum, and other products) within the Strait of Hormuz essentially have only two options," economist David Wech wrote in an email. Wech monitors the flow of energy commodities such as oil and refined products for the British company Vortexa.

"Option 1: to halt production and earn no money at all — or even incur losses due to operating expenditures," Wech wrote. "And option 2: accept the risk of transiting the strait and thereby earn 90% or more of their normal revenue. With an oil price of currently more than $80 per barrel, we're talking about billions of USD."

With hostilities hot again as of July, the Brent Crude oil price is on yet another upward trend, perhaps one of the most perceivable global effects of the war and the near shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz. 

What are alternatives to Strait of Hormuz?

In prewar times, roughly 25% of the global maritime oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative routes have limited capacity to compensate for the loss of oil flow through the strait, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). 

Two pipelines are currently used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz: the UAE's ADCOP and another in Saudi Arabia.

The ADCOP in the United Arab Emirates would allow ships to land and load in the northeastern port of Fujairah and transport oil out of the Persian Gulf without transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

The Abqaiq-Yanbu crude oil pipeline system (East-West Crude Pipeline or Petroline) in Saudi Arabia has some capacity left, the IEA reported in February. Publicly available shipping data for Yanbu show an increase in oil-related ship traffic from May through June, compared with previous years.

"Combined, Yanbu and Fujairah have been able to reroute over 4 million barrels a day of crude from having to pass through the Strait of Hormuz," Smith said. "This has been able to act as a release valve to keep barrels flowing to key customers in Asia — but only offsetting 4 of the total 15 million barrels per day that typically passes through the strait."

The alternative routes have their own risks. Reports are increasing of piracy and attacks on ships by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow choke point between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. "Bab al-Mandeb has the potential to add further supply woes to a global supply picture that is already severely constrained," Smith said. 

So, the release valve to the Strait of Hormuz might soon become a maritime choke point of its own.

Edited by Milan Gagnon and Andreas Becker.

entries.title: Germany news: SPD seeks LGBTQ+ protections in constitution
entries.summary: Germany's center-left wants to add sexual identity to the constitution’s anti-discrimination protections. The push comes as part of the response to a deadly weekend attack near Pride celebrations in Berlin. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: SPD seeks LGBTQ+ protections in constitution

Published July 28, 2026last updated July 28, 2026

Germany's center-left wants to add sexual identity to the constitution’s anti-discrimination protections. The push comes as part of the response to a deadly weekend attack near Pride celebrations in Berlin. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany's Social Democratic Party wants sexual identity added to Article 3 of the German constitution
  • The article already bans discrimination on grounds such as race, religion and sex
  • The conservative CSU wants talks on ankle tags for extremist threats after a deadly attack on a Berlin LGBTQ+ event
  • The suspect in that attack had been sentenced in May for trying to join "Islamic State," but was not immediately jailed
  • Mercedes-Benz vehicle group profits rose for the first time in three years, despite a slump in China sales

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from and about Germany on Tuesday, July 28, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Ebola patient discharged from Frankfurt hospital

Ebola patient discharged from Frankfurt hospital

A patient infected with Ebola has been discharged from Frankfurt University Hospital after making a full recovery.

The US patient had been treated in a specialist isolation unit since mid-July and was able to leave on Tuesday "fully recovered" and "symptom-free," the hospital said.

It was the second US Ebola patient from the Democratic Republic of Congo to be successfully treated in Germany in recent months. The first patient was brought to Berlin's Charité hospital in May and discharged in early June after recovering.

Skip next section IS allegiance video found after Berlin CSD Pride attack

IS allegiance video found after Berlin CSD Pride attack

German investigators have found a video on the phone of suspected Berlin Christopher Street Day Pride attacker Abdul B. in which he pledged allegiance to the "Islamic State" militant terror group.

The Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed a report by the Bild newspaper about the footage. The news magazine "Spiegel" reported that the masked man spoke Arabic in the recording and was believed to be Abdul B.

A woman was killed and 31 people were injured, some seriously, when the suspected attacker drove a car into people near the event on Saturday. He is also suspected of using a machete.

The 21-year-old, who was known as a possible terror threat, died the following day after being shot by police officers who confronted him.

Skip next section Ice cream and water sales surge during German heatwave

Ice cream and water sales surge during German heatwave

People in Germany bought sharply more ice cream and bottled water during the late-June heatwave, according to supermarket checkout data.

Ice cream sales between June 22 and 28 were 90% higher than in an average summer week from 2023 to 2025, the Federal Statistical Office said.

Sales of still water rose by 77%, while sparkling water increased by 63%. All three products reached their highest sales levels since the data series began in early 2023.

Other drinks also sold more strongly. Beer-mix beverages were up 63%, alcohol-free beer 38%, carbonated fruit drinks 34% and cola 32%.

The figures were based on scanner data collected from branches of several major food retailers across Germany.

The heatwave lasted from June 18 to 28 and peaked during the final weekend, according to the German Weather Service.

Skip next section Online vacation bookings hit German record

Online vacation bookings hit German record

Bookings for tourist accommodation in Germany through major online platforms have reached a record high.

Travel patterns varied considerably between Germany's states.

Read more about the story here.

Skip next section Low Rhine levels could push German economy into stagnation

Low Rhine levels could push German economy into stagnation

Persistently low water levels on the Rhine River could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy.

Prolonged dry weather has continued to lower levels on the river, one of the world's busiest inland waterways.

"The effects could be strong enough to reduce gross domestic product in the third quarter by 0.1% to 0.2%," Stefan Kooths, director of the institute's business cycle and growth research group, told the Reuters new agency on Tuesday.

Many economists expect growth of no more than 0.2% during the summer months, meaning the disruption could push Europe's largest economy into stagnation.

At Kaub, a crucial bottleneck between the cities of Koblenz and Mainz, the gauge fell to 30 centimeters (12 inches) on Tuesday. Germany's waterways authority expects it to drop to around 25 centimeters by Friday, matching a record low reached in October 2018.

"As water levels are unlikely to rise suddenly above the critical threshold at the beginning of August, transport capacity is likely to remain impaired for some time next month," Kooths said.

The Rhine carries key commodities including grain, minerals, ores, coal and petroleum products such as petrol.

Skip next section Mercedes profit rises, but car business slumps

Mercedes profit rises, but car business slumps

Mercedes-Benz has reported its first rise in quarterly group profit in three years, although its main car business suffered a sharp fall as sales in China weakened.

The German carmaker's overall net profit rose 13.5% to €1.09 billion ($1.24 billion) between April and June, up from €957 million in the same period last year.

The increase was driven by stronger results from Mercedes' vans and financial services businesses.

But earnings at the company's core passenger-car division fell 26% to €909 million as intense competition and weak demand continued to hit sales in China.

Mercedes also wrote €704 million off the value of its Chinese investments. The non-cash charge indicates that the company expects the difficult market conditions to persist.

Once that write-down is included, profit at the car division fell by almost 94%.

Skip next section Bavarian conservatives seek ankle tags for extremist threats

Bavarian conservatives seek ankle tags for extremist threats

The conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) has called for talks within Germany’s ruling coalition on using electronic ankle tags to monitor people deemed extremist security threats.

The call follows an attack near Berlin's Christopher Street Day LGBTQ+ Pride parade on Saturday.

Alexander Hoffmann, the head of the CSU group in parliament, raised the proposal in an interview with broadcaster Deutschlandfunk. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, also of the CSU, has previously floated the idea.

The CSU is the Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats, who rule with the backing of the center-left Social Democrats.

A woman was killed and 29 people were injured, some seriously, when a vehicle was driven into people near the CSD event.

The 21-year-old suspected attacker, Abdul B., was sentenced in May 2026 to one year and 10 months in juvenile detention for attempting to join the "Islamic State" militant terror group.

However, the sentence was imposed with a provisional form of suspension under juvenile law, so he was not immediately sent to prison. The judgment was also not yet final because prosecutors had appealed

Abdul B. died the day after the attack after being shot by police officers who confronted him.

Skip next section SPD renews push for constitutional protection of LGBTQ+ people

SPD renews push for constitutional protection of LGBTQ+ people

Germany's Social Democrats have renewed calls to add sexual identity to the constitution's anti-discrimination protections following the deadly attack near Berlin's Christopher Street Day LGBTQ+ Pride celebrations.

Center-left Social Democrat (SPD) co-leaders Bärbel Bas and Lars Klingbeil, as well as the party’s General Secretary Tim Klüssendorf said they would put the proposed amendment "firmly back on the political agenda."

"We want to further strengthen the political protection of queer people," they said in a statement seen by the DPA news agency.

The SPD has previously called for sexual identity to be added to Article 3 of Germany's constitution, known as the Basic Law. The article prohibits discrimination on grounds including sex, ancestry, language, origin, faith and political beliefs.

Left Party leader Luigi Pantisano made a similar demand on Monday, saying his party was ready to help secure the two-thirds majority needed in parliament.

Changes to Germany's constitution require a two-thirds majority in both the Bundestag and the Bundesrat, the two chambers of the German parliament.

The governing coalition, led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU bloc, would not have enough votes on its own.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn, where the sun is shining.

You join us as Germany’s Social Democrats revive calls to strengthen constitutional protection for LGBTQ+ people.

Meanwhile, Bavaria’s conservative CSU is pushing for talks on whether electronic ankle tags should be used to monitor people deemed extremist security threats.

Both proposals follow the deadly attack near Berlin’s Christopher Street Day celebrations, in which a woman was killed and 29 people were injured.

Stay with us for these stories and more of the things that Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: India news: Activists decry AI surveillance at CJP protests
entries.summary: A suit has been brought alleging mass surveillance and data collection of "Cockroach" movement protesters. DW has more.
entries.content:
Asia

India news: Activists decry AI surveillance at CJP protests

Published July 28, 2026last updated July 28, 2026

A suit has been brought alleging mass surveillance and data collection of "Cockroach" movement protesters. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A student activist has appealed Delhi's High Court to declare mass surveillance of protesters ​unconstitutional
  • Solicitor General Tushar Mehta defended the Indian police's conduct during the CJP protest
  • The Assam and Bihar governments have agreed to drop charges against some protesters

This blog is now closed. Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Tuesday, July 28:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Court halts demolition of Mohammad Ali Jauhar University in Rampur

Court halts demolition of Mohammad Ali Jauhar University in Rampur

Moradabad Divisional Commissioner’s court on Monday has blocked the proposed demolition of 38 buildings at Mohammad Ali Jauhar University until a final hearing in the case.

A demolition notice was issued for 38 of 40 buildings at Mohammad Ali Jauhar University, which was founded by Samajwadi Party leader Azam Khan in Uttar Pradesh's Rampur city.

The authorities issued the demolition notice saying these structures were constructed without permission.

The university was given 15 days' time to remove the "unauthorized" construction, adding the administration will proceed with the demolition if the institution fails to comply.

Mohammad Ali Jauhar University has been mired in controversy over its acquistion of land, and in 2023 the government of Uttar Pradesh terminated its lease, resulting in a drawn-out court battle.

Skip next section Bihar, Assam to withdraw cases against protesters

Bihar, Assam to withdraw cases against protesters

Hours after the CJP issued a statement over a breach of their demand to withdraw police cases against protesters — the ruling BJP’s Bihar and Assam governments said that all such charges will be dropped and protesters detained before 6 pm on July 26 will be released.

The party's West Bengal government, however, has not given any such assurances.

Union ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh had assured the the party that no action would be taken against peaceful protesters, news agency PTI reported.

In a press release issued by the Home and Political Department the Assam government said five cases had been registered in Assam in connection with the protests, leading to the arrest of 13 people.

"No adverse legal action will be initiated by any of the Police authorities within the State against those persons who have been involved in these protests," the press release said.

The statement said that the process of withdrawing the registered cases, irrespective of the stage of proceedings within Assam, will be initiated promptly as per law.

According to the police, altogether 694 people had been detained for participating in the protests in Bihar.

The Bihar government also announced that it will withdraw all cases lodged against protesters over the NEET paper leak and release those jailed under various charges.

Skip next section Probe finds RAF personnel were issued pellet guns during CJP protest

Probe finds RAF personnel were issued pellet guns during CJP protest

An internal inquiry has found that at least a dozen personnel of the Rapid Action Force (RAF) were issued pellet guns on the morning of July 20 to quell the CJP protests.

The weapons were withdrawn on July 23 after allegations that they were used to harm the protesters, according to a report by Indian newspaper The Hindustan Times.

RAF is a specialized unit within the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) deployed to handle riots and other public disturbances across the country.

Reportedly, five people have alleged that they were hit with pellets on July 20.

The probe has quoted a CRPF inspector as saying that he didn’t issue any order to fire the pellet guns, the officials cited above added.

However, a general diary entry filed at Parliament Street police station reveals that the Rapid Action Force (RAF) fired two rounds from an anti-riot gun on the directions of a Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP) rank officer of the police, as reported by the Indian newspaper The Hindu.

Skip next section Modi government faces challenge from activists over AI use at CJP protest

Modi government faces challenge from activists over AI use at CJP protest

Activists in India have challenged Narendra Modi's government over the use of AI-powered surveillance during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest. 

The controversy erupted when protesters and media reports showed a police surveillance van equipped with cameras on a telescopic mast providing a 360-degree view of the gathering.

Student activist Aishe Ghosh has asked the Delhi High Court to declare mass surveillance of protesters ​unconstitutional.

She also wants the court to order the destruction of all personal data collected during the CJP demonstration.

India has no law governing the use of facial recognition technology by police and surveillance ​at the main protest site in New Delhi was a breach of the law, activists say.

During the case's hearing, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta defended the Indian police conduct, saying privacy claims at a public gathering were "ironical" and the checks were "absolutely necessary" and "in legitimate state interest."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from the New Delhi bureau bringing you the latest news from India.

After witnessing one of the biggest protests in years, people in India woke up to the aftermath of the demonsrations as mass arrests, detentions, and government surveillance made their way to the headlines.

Activists in India have challenged the Indian government over the use of AI-powered surveillance during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests.

However, some state governments have said that the charges against the protesters will be dropped.

Meanwhile, an internal probe has revealed security personnel were issued pellet guns to quell the CJP protest.

Stay tuned as we bring you all this and more from India.

entries.title: Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine seeks stronger air defense
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in the United States to press for stronger military cooperation, as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes amid stalled peace efforts.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine seeks air defense systems

July 28, 2026

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in the United States to press for stronger military cooperation, as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes amid stalled peace efforts.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in the United States ahead of talks with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, saying Kyiv's top priority was securing stronger air defense and strategic cooperation as Russia intensified attacks.

"Our number-one priority is anti-ballistic defense and strategic cooperation with America. Peace needs to be brought closer," Zelenskyy said in a post on X after arriving in the US.

The two leaders are due to meet at the White House before attending a tribute to Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, who passed away earlier this month.

US-Ukraine ties improving

The long-strained relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have improved in recent weeks.

Since returning to office in January last year, Trump largely stopped direct US arms shipments to Ukraine, instead allowing European allies to buy American weapons and supply them to Kyiv.

However, Washington remains a key ally, providing intelligence and access to the Starlink satellite network used by Ukrainian frontline troops to communicate.

In a sign of improving ties, Trump, in a meeting with Zelenskyy in Turkey earlier this month, pledged to help Ukraine produce Patriot air defense systems, saying Kyiv would be able to produce them "pretty quickly."

This has been a long-running request from Kyiv in order to counter Russian missile attacks.

Kyiv and Moscow ramp up long-range strikes

The Trump-Zelenskyy meeting comes as more than four years have passed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war, both sides have stepped up long-range strikes.

Russia said on Tuesday that more than 390 Ukrainian drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, damaging residential buildings.

Russian state media also reported that Russian forces struck two vessels, including a ship in the Black Sea that Moscow claimed was transporting military supplies for Ukraine, according to Reuters.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
